what_its_for: Insulin lispro-aabc is a fast-acting insulin used to control blood sugar (glucose) levels in adults and children with diabetes. It helps your body use the sugar from the food you eat. It is used at mealtimes to prevent blood sugar from rising too high after eating.
how_to_take: Inject insulin lispro-aabc under the skin (subcutaneous injection) in your stomach area (abdomen), upper arms, thighs, or buttocks. Rotate your injection sites each time to help prevent skin problems. You can also receive it through a continuous subcutaneous insulin pump. Never inject it into a vein or muscle on your own. Always wash your hands before preparing and giving your injection. Check the insulin — it should be clear and colorless. Do not use it if it looks cloudy, colored, or has particles in it.
dosing: Your doctor will set your dose based on your individual blood sugar levels, meal size, and overall diabetes management plan. Inject it right before a meal (within 2 minutes of starting to eat) or up to 20 minutes after starting a meal. Your dose will be different from other patients — never share your insulin pen or syringe with anyone else, even if the needle has been changed. Follow your doctor's instructions exactly.
missed_dose: If you forget to inject insulin lispro-aabc before your meal, you may take it up to 20 minutes after you start eating, as long as you remember during that same meal. If the meal is over and more than 20 minutes have passed, skip that dose. Never double up on doses to make up for a missed one. Check your blood sugar as directed and contact your healthcare provider if you are unsure what to do.
storage: Store unopened (unused) insulin pens or vials in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze insulin — throw it away if it has been frozen. Keep it away from direct heat and sunlight. Once you begin using a vial or pen, you may store it at room temperature (below 77°F / 25°C) for up to 28 days. Always check the expiration date on the label and throw it away after the expiration date or after 28 days of first use, whichever comes first. Keep all insulin out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol, as it can cause unpredictable changes in your blood sugar and increase your risk of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Do not skip meals after taking your dose, as this can cause dangerously low blood sugar. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if your blood sugar is low or if you feel dizzy or confused. Do not mix insulin lispro-aabc with other insulins in the same syringe unless your doctor has specifically told you to. Avoid changing your brand of insulin or pen without talking to your doctor or pharmacist first.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience signs of very low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) such as shakiness, sweating, fast heartbeat, dizziness, confusion, extreme hunger, or fainting. Also call your doctor if you notice signs of high blood sugar (hyperglycemia) such as increased thirst, frequent urination, blurred vision, or fatigue. Seek emergency help for signs of a serious allergic reaction, including rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing, or a fast heartbeat. Tell your doctor if you notice skin thickening, pitting, or lumps at your injection sites.
when_it_works: Insulin lispro-aabc starts working very quickly — usually within about 15 to 30 minutes after injection. It reaches its peak effect (works the hardest) in about 30 to 90 minutes. Its blood sugar-lowering effect lasts for approximately 3 to 5 hours. Because it works so fast, it is important to eat your meal right away after injecting.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Insulin needs often change during pregnancy and after delivery, and close monitoring is very important. Older adults (65 years and older): Older patients may be at higher risk for low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Your doctor may start you on a lower dose and monitor you more carefully. Children: Insulin lispro-aabc can be used in children with type 1 diabetes. Doses are based on the child's weight and blood sugar levels and must be set by a doctor. Kidney or liver disease: Your insulin dose may need to be adjusted if you have kidney or liver problems, as these conditions can affect how your body responds to insulin. Always inform your entire healthcare team of all medical conditions and all medications you are taking.
